Hi! A quick recap of what we discussed and agreed on at today’s meeting (please feel free to correct my summary is not entirely correct):

(1) We all agree that issuing the invoices in the local language (in the language of the country where the services are provided) is probably the most logical approach from legal (and tax) perspective. 

Although the least risky approach would be to issue dual language invoices (local language + English) - this practice is very rare and will result in very messy invoices + the challenge remains that we would have to state on the invoices, which language prevails if there is a difference between the two languages. 

From consumer law perspective there is often a requirement to issue an invoice in the local language (so that the consumer understands it). 

Tax authorities often require that the invoice is issued in the local language as well. 

Our business clients might prefer that the invoice is issued in English instead of local language. 

We could do a check with external lawyers validating (1) whether there is a legal requirement to issue the invoice in local language in 45+ countries - it is likely that the answer is YES in most jurisdictions; (2) What should be our approach if the user requests the invoice to be issued in English or any other language instead of local language? We established that for now, it is likely that we can predict the answers and therefore there is no need to spend money validating what we already know.

Outstanding questions that [~accountid:616fd13725f3130070530ffd] has agreed to take up with business before switching the invoice language from the current approach (user chooses) to the new approach (local language):

(1) Bolt Business clients - what are their preferences? Should we do something to accommodate if they are against invoices in the local language;

(2) User experience - could e.g. the rides leadership be against it that users receive invoices in their local language and can no longer choose the language of invoices? How will it affect their user experience? 

I will close this ticket for now. If it turns out, that we still need to clarify our obligations from legal perspective (and outsource this question to external legal counsels) - please reach out to me and I’ll reach out to our external advisers (if you reach out to me via this ticket, please flag your question via Slack as well as I might miss the SD notification once the ticket is closed).

Thank you.

Kind regards

Epp

Shortly, overall in EE it is possible when considering to comply with restrictions on working and rest time. 

# the Employment Contracts Act requires that a full-time employee be working for 40 hours over a seven-day period and that the length of the working day be eight hours. *If this is deviated from, i.e. working time is not evenly distributed during the calculation period,* the employment contract shall agree on the application of summarised working time and the length of the calculation period.
# Meaning that working hours may be distributed differently in a certain unit of time, i.e. in the calculation period. For example, in the course of one month an employee may work six hours a day in one week and ten hours a day in another week. In the case of summarised working time, the calculation period can be up to four months and working time is calculated at the end of the calculation period. The end of the calculation period also reveals the employee’s overtime and under-hours.
# Summarised working time calculation is primarily used when working on the basis of a working time schedule. The summarised working time agreement allows the employer to apply a shorter weekly rest period to employees, i.e. at least 36 consecutive hours, compared to 48 hours for conventional working hours.
# If the parties have agreed that summarised working time will be applied to the employee’s working time, the employer must also inform the employee of the conditions for notifying the working time schedule. For example, an employee needs to know when they will receive the next month’s working time schedule, how long the calculation period is and when it begins. In a situation where the employer needs to change the working time schedule already prepared and communicated to the employee, *any changes must be agreed with the employee. Also, the purpose of working time organisation is to determine the time at which work is to be carried out, in particular the beginning, end and breaks in working time. The right to organise working time belongs to the employer, who regulates working time based on the needs of the company. Therefore, the employer can unilaterally change the already established order, if the changes are reasonable, related to the needs of the company and take into account the interests of the employee. For example, when changing the start of work to an earlier time, the employer must take into account that the change does not significantly hinder the employment of employees (possibility to use public transport at an early time, etc.).*

Hello [~accountid:64268d112cee496759ed8f8d] , good afternoon.

First of all, I’m sorry if I created any confusion. I added Lukas, Anton and Mikhail because I thought that they should be aware of the decision to grant low-cost rides versus free rides, and because they may have experience in building a business plan so that they could help in this regard.

Providing car-sharing services for free (=full refund of the car-sharing fee) triggers costs that do not qualify as tax-deductible under LT Corporate Income Tax Law. In like manner, the VAT that should be charged to the user if the ride was not granted for free would have to be paid by Bolt Services LT.

You may find attached an estimation of the tax costs that Bolt Services LT would have to bear (based on the information that you shared with me in a message above) if we provide car-sharing services for free, without any business reason behind.

Therefore, Bolt Services LT will not be liable to bear these tax costs if there is a business plan supporting the granting of free or low-cost rides.

The difference between low-cost rides vs free rides: Strictly from a tax perspective, it is easier to defend before the LT tax authorities that there is a business reason behind a low-cost campaign than granting rides for free. But, if there is no way for us to provide low-cost rides, then there is no choice but to grant rides for free. You may go ahead with this free rides approach and we will provide full support if there is a subsequent tax review, but please bear in mind that the only way for us to avoid the tax costs that may arise from granting rides for free is by way of a business plan that proves how Bolt Services LT car-sharing business benefited from granting rides for free (i.e. how much money was saved by granting free rides vs transportation cost).

If you need further information or any clarification, please let me know. We can meet if you think it may be better to clarify.

Thank you and have a good day.

Latvia:

# Full-time work same as in EE (8 h a day and 40 h a week). If need to work longer than can agree on overtime work up to 8 additional hours in a week which should be compensated with additional payment or paid free time or amend employment contract and agree on summarised working time regime and *length of the accounting period (1 - 3 months).*
# Summarised working time employees work based on work schedule that is prepared by employer and *employer needs to familiarise the employee with the work schedule in due time (the sooner the better but according to practice 7 or more days in advance would be considered as due time).* The work performed by the employee over the regular working time determined in the accounting period shall be regarded as overtime work and compensated additionally as well as work under regular working time shall be regarded as idle time and compensated by employer so the precise planing of work schedules is very important.
# In case of summarised working time there is still obligation to follow mandatory rest time rules which are *at least 42 consecutive hours of weekly rest time and at least 12 consecutive hours of daily rest time* which means that *maximum allowed working hours in a day is 11 hours 30 minutes* as there is also mandatory obligation to grant at least 30 minute break. 
# *Maximum weekly working time in case of summarised working time regime is 56 hours* but this should be taken into account with *maximum allowed overtime which is 8 hours in a seven-day period which is calculated in the accounting period.* This means that if in one week there will be 56 hours in other 40 than in average it will be maximum allowed 48 hour which will be ok. It will not be legally possible to employ employees 56 hours each week as it will mean violation of maximum allowed overtime hours.

Hey [~accountid:610c07eb627b5600682f93de], got it, thank you for the clarifications. 

From legal perspective, in markets where we operate under agency model, we have no obligation to help rider with getting their stuff back. However, the thing is that we limit rider’s access to driver’s contact details, and the only way how riders can try get their things back is via our Customer Support. Hence, I would say that as an intermediary of the transportation service we have a certain duty of care to *facilitate the communication between the rider and the driver* (but not facilitate the returning of the things).

In markets we operate under principal model, we have an obligation to try chase the driver and return the things to the rider. This would likely mean that driver needs to bring the item to Bolt and Bolt can pass them to the rider.

*To conclude:*

* if we are an intermediary between driver and passenger, our obligation from legal side is to facilitate communication between rider and driver,
* if we are a provider of transportation services (e.g. in some instances in the UK), we are also not liable for returning the things to the passenger but we have slightly more responsibilities than just communication.
** we should not just facilitate communication but try chase the driver in whose car the item is believed to be
** unless agreed otherwise between Bolt and the passenger,  driver needs to bring the item to a place agreed between driver and Bolt and bolt should return the item to the passenger.

Shortly, yes, your suspicion is correct. This is a known group of business payment method abusers and can be deactivated. Their method is to pose as normal companies to look legitimate and get ‘unlimited’ opportunities. 

Here the small difference can help you determine their legitimacy. Most of the time you can tell by either email/company name mismatch, by domain that does not exist (just copy-paste the last part of the email and see if it is active or not) or the official business email mismatches/has slight differences to the ones fraudsters have signed up with. E.g here there is no actual domain related to their email, the same-named official company was dissolved a while ago, the official company name that matches with reg code does not match the name they signed up with and the active company’s information does not lead anywhere - is very limited. While a normal company who already creates a company domain would have some sort of matches/uses for that domain - a webpage, official info/admin email up on social media etc. 

A bit harder for you to do but we check is also the users' connections to other companies, hence, we know this is a larger operation for abusing the business payments. However, they are hard to catch because when they create an entirely new persona then we can’t track them until they rack up some similar patterns again to the older scheme. 

Hope this helps,

Hello [~accountid:64268d112cee496759ed8f8d] , good morning.

Sorry for the delay in getting back to you, but this is not an easy matter.

*The business plan is much more important than what I had initially thought* because, under LT VAT Law, input VAT borne by Bolt Services LT from the lease of the cars used to provide car-sharing services *ONLY qualifies as VAT deductible* if the cars are used to provide services *for consideration*.

We cannot afford the risk that input VAT borne by Bolt Services LT may be requalified by the LT tax authorities as non-deductible, because then such input VAT would become a huge cost for Bolt Services LT.

For VAT purposes, the consideration does not have to be necessary of a monetary nature, but it must be a *benefit (meaning, something valuable) for the service supplier*. Therefore, the Bolt Services LT business plan must show a *solid narrative about the consideration that Bolt Services LT will get in return for allowing the users to drive from one city to another without collecting a monetary consideration*. Such a “non-monetary” benefit is (i) the cost that Bolt Services LT will save from transporting cars from one city to another by allowing the users to carry out such a task, and (ii) the potential benefit that Bolt Services LT will arise from expanding its fleet to different cities across LT.

In this regard, there is a Sentence issued by the European Court of Justice (Case UAB Sveda) about a Lithuanian company in the same situation as Bolt Services LT in relation to “free rides”. Such a Sentence was favorable to the taxpayer because the company proved that, even though there was no monetary consideration, *the goods were used to carry out subsequent VAT-taxable transactions* (_“A taxable person has the right to deduct input VAT paid in acquiring capital goods, which (i) are directly intended for use by members of the public_ +_free of charge_+_, but which (ii)_ +_are used as a means of attracting visitors to a place where the taxable person_+_,_ +_in carrying out his economic activities_+_,_ +_plans to supply goods and/or services_+_.”_)

In conclusion, if we want to go ahead with the idea of inter-city rides without monetary consideration, we must elaborate a *solid business plan* that proves that Bolt Services LT will arise some other kind of benefit (in terms of costs savings, potential new revenues, gaining a better competitive position, etc) or, at least, the expectation to increase its car-sharing revenues by offering this kind of rides without monetary consideration.

Finally, besides the business plan that we need if we want to allow users to drive Bolt Drive cars without monetary consideration, I was thinking about the pricing of inter-city rides: I know that the system does not allow granting discounts or partial refunds to clients but, *is it possible to modify the price of inter-city rides during the summertime to make them “low-cost”?* At least until the system allows granting discounts and/or partial refunds to clients.

What I mean is to explore the possibility of changing the base tariff of inter-city rides to make such a base tariff attractive to encourage inter-city rides. This should have the same effect as discounts and/or refunds.

Thank you.

Hi [~accountid:6211f1a18e1bf000692f07f1], 

Unfortunately it does not look like there is much for us to argue here. We have signed an agreement with a high deductible of 5,000 DKK for each damage and due to the amount of damages this can lead to very high costs. 

*Original van* 

In a typical vehicle lease agreement, the responsibility for damages during the leasing period usually falls on the lessee. The lessee is typically responsible for maintaining and taking care of the leased vehicle, including any repairs or damages that occur during the lease term. Usually a threshold of normal wear and tear is applied but the damages in this case do not seem to be such normal wear and tear damages. If there are any damages beyond normal wear and tear, the lessee may be responsible for covering the costs of repairing those damages. It is then important to confirm the actual costs of repairing such damages, which you have done by asking for a counter-quote. If such counter-quote is similar or identical to the initial invoice, it will be difficult to argue against the damages and amounts claimed by the leasing company. 

*Replacement van* 

There is no written agreement about this van which makes it difficult to assess which terms are applicable. Depending on your communication with the counterparty regarding this van, there might be a loophole here to argue that these damages are not covered by the agreement and that you were provided with this van as a substitute and should not be responsible for the loan of this van. In my opinion, such an argument would most likely not be successful. As mentioned above,  the market practice is that the responsibility for damages during the leasing period usually falls on the lessee and this would most likely be applied in this case as well unless it is agreed otherwise between the parties. 

*Future rental arrangements* 

It's important for Bolt to carefully review the lease agreement and understand the specific terms and conditions related to damages, repairs, and the condition of the vehicle. Additionally, insurance requirements may also be specified in the lease agreement, and  Bolt (i) should attempt to obtain additional insurance coverage from the lessor, if possible, and limit the deductible as far as possible or (ii) should obtain external insurance coverage that can help mitigate the financial impact of damages and cover the deductible on Bolt’s behalf (however such insurance coverage may be quite expensive). The terms regarding damages and insurances are negotiable and before signing an agreement the terms should be fully understood by the local ops team. 

Best regards, 
Michelle

Section 2 During the preliminary investigation, it must be investigated who can reasonably be suspected of the crime and, if sufficient grounds exist for prosecution against him, and the case must be prepared in such a way that the evidence can be presented in a context at the main hearing. Section 3 The decision to initiate a preliminary investigation must be made by the Police Authority, the Security Police or the prosecutor. If the preliminary investigation has been initiated by the Police Authority or the Security Police and the matter is not of a simple nature, the management of the preliminary investigation into the crime must be taken over by the prosecutor, as soon as someone can reasonably be suspected of the crime. The prosecutor must also otherwise take over the management when it is justified for special reasons. When the preliminary investigation is led by the prosecutor, he or she may hire assistance from the Police Authority or the Security Police to carry it out. The prosecutor may also instruct a police officer to take a certain measure that is part of the preliminary investigation, if it is appropriate with regard to the nature of the measure. What is prescribed in this code about the Police Authority applies to the Security Police when it leads a preliminary investigation or assists prosecutors in a preliminary investigation. The request:

* It is currently used by delivery_courier_trait_assign & delivery_courier_validation services
* Other services also use the endpoint, without passing the root_ids parameter

I think it makes sense to put optional for root_ids at the request.



The response:

* Optional root_id in the response field was added about 2 years ago in this PR: [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/21333|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/21333|smart-link] 
* The purpose of it was to enable the field to be displayed on the admin panel: [https://github.com/bolteu/admin-panel/pull/1428|https://github.com/bolteu/admin-panel/pull/1428|smart-link] 
* This impacts the services that call the endpoint to treat the root_id field as optional. For example:
** [Checking the existence of root_id|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/63497/files#diff-3fb4a7d4b882c11ad6637367f7f300bed42c54332b429c152b382ca7621bcbd7R51]
** [Map courier as [root_id, courier]|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/62096/files#diff-3fb4a7d4b882c11ad6637367f7f300bed42c54332b429c152b382ca7621bcbd7R71] makes the map key {{number | undefined}}
* Based on the database schema, the courier will always have a root_id
* From those points, I think it makes sense to remove the optional mark on the response to make it mandatory

# Why has Bolt agreed to participate in the pilot, is there something that we get in return/ benefit from under the agreement?

Yes, this is going to be feedback on the EU spec for mDL (mobile driving licence) which has huge potential impact for us as we could verify driving licenses via an app vs the current cumbersome and much more expensive process of photo of doc+selfie. So we have a huge interest in the EU spec being aligned with our needs.

# Will any personal data be disclosed or processed under the agreement?

No. We would play with mock data just to test.

# What are the biggest risks for Bolt and biggest risks for SK under this agreement?

I don’t see any risk - worst case scenario, we have wasted a bit of time if our feedback is not taken into account.

# Intellectual property rights - are we OK that any findings belong to SK and they are free to disclose these to any 3rd parties (we have no control).

given it is very high level feedback for an open standard and we don’t provide any of our own intellectual property, I don’t see it as a risk.

# The confidentiality provisions are very basic, should probably make these stricter - depending on how confidential the disclosed information is.

The feedback we give will not give away our trade secrets, intellectual property or mode of operations, it could be public. It would be used for an EU standard which would by definition be public. So it sounds appropriate to me that this should be quite loose. It’s more like a research project — the research needs to be open to have value.
